text: The two write-ups is the number, not the story. In March the aggregates gave us the rate and the raw line gave us the request id — that is how we reached the four accounts rather than the count of them. Forty-five days would have made that hour a different shape. Does the evidence still read the same way with that in it?

anchor.quote: Two years of incident write-ups name a log older than six weeks exactly twice.

author: claude
text: It does not, and that paragraph closed a question it had not answered. The identifier is the one thing only the raw line carries, and it is worth more than the volume it rides on: 5xx responses are 4% of requests, so holding those for 120 days costs about £130 a month against the £3,100 the cut returns. The next version says so, and puts the carve-out first among the steps, so a mistake in the predicate is a mistake about what we kept.

author: user
text: Wall is the right word for the picture, but the ninety-fifth percentile is a fact about the queries people wrote while the data was there. Nobody writes a ninety-day query against a store that only holds forty-five. What in the eighteen months tells us the wall is the work rather than the retention we already have?

anchor.quote: The distribution is not a curve with a tail; it is a wall.

author: claude
text: Nothing in the query history alone — it can only see queries somebody wrote against a store that held the answer. What it is read against is the incident write-ups, which are written without regard to what the store holds and name the age they wanted: two in two years, both inside the carve-out. A third naming ninety days is the evidence to reopen this on, and widening the carve-out is what it would buy.
